title: Yara and the Ledger
premise: In the waning years of a border war, Casper Dunmore, a battlefield nurse, secretly records in a ledger the names of soldiers and civilians that official reports erase. When a census taker named Yara arrives asking questions about a village officially declared empty, Casper realizes the ledger is the only proof its people ever existed — including Marisol, a healer now branded an enemy who once saved Casper's life. Pursued by an officer determined to burn the record and the village's last survivors with it, Casper and Yara carry the ledger across occupied country to reach a neutral tribunal before the amnesty deadline expires. The book ends with the names read aloud into the official record at great personal cost: Casper loses their post and their country's protection, but gains a new belonging among the people they refused to let vanish.
about_author: O. M. Villalobos is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing displaced-persons records from forgotten border conflicts. They write historical fiction about the paperwork of war — the lists, ledgers, and omissions that decide who gets remembered.

chapters.title: What the Orders Weigh
chapters.summary: Casper Dunmore's POV. In a field hospital on the eve of evacuation, Casper triages patients by what can be carried when the orders come, and quietly enters three unrecorded dead into a worn ledger. The emotional beat is weary tenderness — care as an act of accounting no one asked for.

chapters.title: The Census Taker
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Yara arrives at the hospital under government seal, counting heads for a census that will determine rations and repatriation. She asks one question too many: whether anyone from Vellamora village passed through. Casper lies badly, and Yara notices. Beat: wary mutual recognition between two people who count things.

chapters.title: Marisol's Hands
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Casper's POV. Three years earlier, in peacetime, a Vellamoran healer named Marisol saved Casper's shattered arm when no army surgeon would touch a foreigner. Casper promised her the ledger would hold her name if war ever came. Beat: the promise that will cost everything.

chapters.title: Empty on Paper
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. In the census office, Yara discovers Vellamora has been struck from every map and register — declared enemy territory, its population legally nonexistent. Her superior orders her to certify the emptiness. Beat: the quiet horror of bureaucratic erasure.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Instead of certifying, Yara files an inquiry, drawing the attention of Major Aldous Renk, the officer who authored Vellamora's erasure. He offers her promotion for silence. Beat: loyalty to the institution begins to crack against loyalty to truth.

chapters.title: The Ledger Opens
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Yara tracks Casper down and asks directly about Vellamora. Casper shows her the ledger — four hundred names the officers omitted, Marisol's among them. Beat: trust extended as a gamble; two strangers become conspirators.

chapters.title: Renk Learns to Read
chapters.summary: Renk's POV. A bribed orderly reports the ledger's existence. Renk, whose career rests on Vellamora's nonexistence, orders the hospital searched and Casper watched. Beat: cold menace; the antagonist revealed as a man protecting a lie he cannot survive admitting.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. With the search imminent, Casper must choose what to carry when the orders come again — this time fleeing ones. They take the ledger, a scalpel, and nothing else, leaving behind rank, wages, and safety. Beat: severance; the theme made literal.

chapters.title: The Road Out of the Map
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Casper and Yara travel unmarked roads toward Vellamora, dodging checkpoints using Yara's census credentials. They argue about whether institutions can be reformed or only survived. Beat: uneasy partnership deepening into respect.

chapters.title: Vellamora Still Breathes
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. They find the village not empty but hiding — forty-one survivors sheltering in cellars and orchard caves, Marisol among them, tending the wounded of both armies. Beat: grief transfigured into fierce, fragile hope.

chapters.title: Forty-One Names
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol reads the ledger and finds her own name written in Casper's careful hand. She reveals the tribunal in neutral Corvane will hear claims until the amnesty deadline — nineteen days away — but only for persons who legally exist. Beat: the promise honored becomes a race against law itself.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara calculates the route: mountains, a flooded river, two garrisons. Renk has posted descriptions of them both. The villagers vote to send five walkers, not all. Beat: dread braided with resolve; the clock starts.

chapters.title: The Orchard Ambush
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Renk's patrol raids the village seeking the ledger. Casper trades their medical kit for the survivors' escape window and takes a bullet graze. Beat: sacrifice; the first blood Casper sheds for paper and ink.

chapters.title: River of Forgetting
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Crossing the flooded river, one walker — old Tomás, the village's oldest memory-keeper — is swept away saving the ledger. His death makes the book heavier than paper. Beat: mourning sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: The Garrison at Kell Bridge
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. To pass the garrison, Yara uses her real credentials one last time, knowing it will end her career and mark her a traitor. She signs her own name into Casper's ledger — the first name added in freedom rather than erasure. Beat: irrevocable choice; loyalty transferred from state to truth.

chapters.title: Renk's Offer
chapters.summary: Renk's POV. Renk corners them at a waystation and offers amnesty for everyone — if the ledger burns and Vellamora stays empty. He confesses, privately, that he erased the village to cover a massacre ordered by his superiors. Beat: the villain humanized without excused; temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: What Casper Carries Now
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper refuses — not with heroics but with arithmetic: four hundred names against one man's career. Renk arrests them. In a cell, Casper memorizes the ledger in case it is seized. Beat: stillness before the storm; memory as the final backup.

chapters.title: The Burning
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Renk burns the captured ledger publicly as a warning. But Marisol and the villagers have copied every name into embroidery, song, and schoolroom slates — the ledger was never only paper. Beat: despair inverted; erasure fails because memory was distributed.

chapters.title: Corvane Gates
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Released through a bribe arranged by sympathetic clerks Yara once counted honestly, the group reaches Corvane with hours left. The tribunal clerk says oral testimony requires a citizen sponsor — and Yara renounces her citizenship to stand sponsor for the dead. Beat: climax threshold; everything staked.

chapters.title: Reading the Names
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Before the tribunal, Casper recites all four hundred names from memory while Marisol and the villagers confirm each with testimony. Renk arrives to discredit them but collapses when his own superiors disown him to save themselves. Beat: climax; justice spoken outside the law's original intention, inside it despite everything.

chapters.title: Amnesty and Its Price
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The tribunal restores Vellamora to the maps and grants its people legal existence; Renk is arrested by his own side. Casper and Yara are stateless now — pardoned by history, punished by paperwork. Beat: bittersweet victory; the cost tallied honestly.

chapters.title: A New Ledger
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, epilogue. In rebuilt Vellamora, Casper opens a fresh ledger and writes the living first: Marisol, Yara, the forty-one, then Tomás. Belonging, they finally understand, is not granted by any census — it is carried, name by name, by those who refuse to put it down. Beat: resolution; the theme closed like a book, opened like a door.
